The World Today · ABC listen

US and China send mixed messages

Broadcast Monday, 9 April 2001 · Reporter: Michael Carey

← Full The World Today episode — Monday, 9 April 2001

COMPERE: What does China want? Well that question is exercising minds at the Pentagon, the White House and the US State Department today.

Everybody thought that 24 men and women from the downed spy plane, the EP-3, would be on their way home to a hero's welcome by now. Instead the air crew remained confined on the ground in Hainan.

Here's Washington correspondent, Michael Carey.

MICHAEL CAREY: With White House officials anxious at what they're calling the mixed signals coming from Beijing, Washington has decided to send some dual track messages as well.

On the one hand, Secretary Powell's warning this morning that each day that passed without the return of the EP-3 crew now on Hainan Island, is a day with a cost to the US-China relationship which could show up in Congressional negotiations on trade, defence, and Taiwan.

On the other hand, statements of sorrow at the loss of the Chinese pilot in the collision which preceded the spy plane's landing in China.

President Bush is writing to the pilot's bereaved wife to offer condolences.

According to Douglas Paul, director of the Asia Pacific Policy Centre the administration is still pinning its hopes on a smooth resolution and a quick release of its personnel. But, he says, the doubts are creeping in.

DOUGLAS PAUL: The expectation was that this would be resolved by Monday based on previous conversations I've had with both Chinese officials and American officials. That's going to be hard to do now, we're down to the last few hours of China for Monday. If it goes on until Wednesday, many politicians here, and I spent yesterday afternoon talking to a bunch of them, many politicians here will start cranking up the pressure on China and the price could start getting quite high for hanging on to these people as long as China is doing so.

MICHAEL CAREY: How vivid within China is the notion that pushing this too far could have real costs?

DOUGLAS PAUL: Well the magical turning point last week came when it stopped being a debating forum between the United States President and the White House and the Chinese military, but the State Department got down to actual negotiations with their counterparts in the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

The US State Department and the Chinese Ministry both have a stake in the relationship with each other. The Chinese military doesn't have any stake in the US relationship and this doesn't proceed one, and it's easy for them to keep raising the ante for a resolution because it helps to keep the public and the budget moving in their direction.

But the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is the organisation that has to take the heat when trade problems arise and other concerns dominate US-China relations.

MICHAEL CAREY: If there isn't a resolution by the middle of this week what is the US actually going to do. How straight forward are the options for the White House?

DOUGLAS PAUL: Well the first thing that comes up is the United Nations Human Rights Commission meeting in Geneva, and the US can significantly crank up the [indistinct] activity and start squeezing its allies to not vote with the Chinese on their motion for non-action which can lead to a national vote against China for the fist time since 1989 and the Tiananmen incident.

The next step that comes up will be on sales decisions with respect to Taiwan and they could become a lot tougher if there isn't a better atmosphere developing, much as Washington would like to separate these two issues, they tend to flow into one another.

COMPERE: Douglas Paul is the director of the Asia Pacific Policy Centre in Washington DC and he was speaking to Michael Carey.
